prime.problem: The readings on coding agents come from different angles (a loop, an API's message format, context engineering, benchmark statistics) and it's easy to lose how they connect. This card puts all four on one page, so each reading has a place to land.
prime.fits: The map for the course: read it first to see the four parts, or last as a recap. Each row and label links to the card that shows the arithmetic.
expect: total input = N × P + Δ × N(N − 1) ÷ 2
four levers: tool output, what's in each call, how the loop ends, measuring
prime.goal: Name the four parts of a harness, place each lever on the formula (N, P or Δ), and say which card to read before which set of readings.

attend: Which term of the formula grows with the square of the number of calls, and which cards shrink it?
In the mental model, where do skills and MCP tools sit, and where does a subagent's work happen?
Why does the ranking include levers that don't make the agent faster or cheaper at all?
When is an agent loop the wrong tool, according to the takeaway?

must: Every call re-sends a stable prefix plus the history → total input = N × P + Δ × N(N − 1) ÷ 2 → the call count N and the per-turn growth Δ matter most on long runs
Each lever touches one term → tool output shrinks Δ, a stable prefix and compaction tame P and the history, budgets and stop reasons bound N → name the term before picking the fix
A change that looks better may be luck → repeats, an interval and hidden tests separate real wins → measure one change at a time
reference: which field guide station matches which card

compress.prompt: Close the card and draw the mental model: the request stack, the model, the tool run, the arrow back, the stop box and the eval strip underneath. Then write the formula and label N, P and Δ with the card that explains each.
checklist: request = tools + system + CLAUDE.md + skill list + history + newest result
model writes tool_use → harness runs it → result appended → call again, or stop
N: agent loop; P: what the model sees; Δ: tool call
eval: fixed tasks × 3 trials → hidden tests → pass rate ± range → $ per solved task

retrieve.q: Explain what the harness decides that the model can't, and give one example from each of the four cards.
answer: the loop and when it ends (budgets, stop reasons)
what each tool sends back (truncation, error messages)
what goes into each call (order, compaction)
how the agent is measured (hidden tests, repeats)

retrieve.q: Use the formula to explain why cutting one tool's output helps more the earlier it happens in a run.
answer: a tool result joins the history and is re-sent on every later call
an early result rides on more calls than a late one
so the saving is its size times the number of calls after it

retrieve.q: You can spend a day on one thing: a better tool output format, a stable-prefix fix, or building a 10-task eval. Which first, and why?
answer: the eval first if you can't yet tell whether any change helps
without it, the other two are guesses
keep it small (tens of tasks) and accept that only big effects will show

compare.q: The speed course's agents overview ranked levers by time to a correct result; this one ranks by tokens, cost and trust in the result. Which lever appears in both, and why?
answer: caching the stable prefix and compacting history appear in both
they cut both the tokens re-read each call and the prefill time
checking each step there, hidden tests here: both are about knowing the result is right

predict.q: Keep P = 4,500 and N = 6 but double Δ from 1,800 to 3,600 (bigger tool outputs). Predict the new total input before computing: about 1.5× or about 2× the 54,000?
predict.answer: 6 × 4,500 + 3,600 × 15 = 27,000 + 54,000 = 81,000 tokens, 1.5×. Only the history term doubles; the prefix term stays at 27,000. On a longer run the history term dominates, so doubling Δ would get closer to 2×.

apply.task: For an agent you use, estimate N (calls in a typical task), P (the stable prefix) and Δ (tokens added per turn). Plug them into the formula, then say which of the four cards' levers would cut the total most and by roughly how much.
apply.done: You have numbers for N, P and Δ, a computed total, one chosen lever, and a before/after estimate.
apply.hint: If Δ is dominated by one tool's output, the tool-call card's truncation is usually the cheapest fix.

reflect: Did you predict 1.5× or 2× for doubling Δ?
